# In Praise of Lichen

Almost every old gravestone carries a crust of pale green, or rusty orange, or a grey that looks like dried paint. Most people who notice it at all think of it as dirt, or a stain, or maybe a kind of moss. It is none of those things. It is a lichen, and it is one of the strangest living things on Earth. It is also, arguably, not a thing at all.

For most of the history of botany, lichens were classified as plants, a single organism with a single name. Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that struck his colleagues as absurd, even offensive. He argued that a lichen is two organisms: a fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus builds the structure, the architecture of the thing, and the alga, tucked inside, photosynthesizes and feeds the household.

The lichenologists of the day hated this idea. Some of the resistance was ordinary scientific conservatism, but some of it was almost moral. Schwendener described the relationship in terms of masters and slaves, the fungus as an exploiter holding the alga captive, and his critics found the whole picture grotesque. A lichen was supposed to be a humble, honest little plant, not a hostage situation. Over the following decades, though, the evidence became overwhelming. Scientists separated the partners and grew them apart. The dual hypothesis won.

It is worth pausing on what was at stake. The word *symbiosis*, in its biological sense, was developed largely to describe lichens. Before we had a vocabulary for organisms that live together in deep mutual dependence, lichens forced us to invent one. Much of how we now think about coral reefs, the mitochondria in our own cells, and the bacteria in our guts traces back, conceptually, to people squinting at crusty growths on rocks and realizing that the individual was not as simple as they had assumed.

The story didn't end in the nineteenth century, either. In 2016, researchers reported that many lichens contain a third partner, a yeast living in the outer layer, which had gone unnoticed for about a hundred and fifty years despite intense study. The lichen, it turned out, was not a couple but something more like a small community, and in some cases the membership is larger still. Each time we look closer, the boundaries of the "organism" blur further.

I find this deeply appealing, and I think the reason is that lichens embarrass our instinct to count things. We like our living world divided into units: one tree, one bird, one person. Lichens refuse this. Ask how many organisms are on that gravestone and the honest answer is something like "it depends on what you mean," which is a frustrating answer and also, I suspect, the correct one for far more of biology than we usually admit.

Then there is the matter of time. Lichens are slow in a way that is hard to take in. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, which forms yellow-green patches with black borders so that a rock covered in them looks like an atlas, can grow less than a millimeter a year. Geologists use this slowness as a clock. By measuring the diameter of the largest lichens on a rock surface, they can estimate how long it has been since that surface was exposed, when a glacier retreated, say, or a rockfall occurred. The technique is called lichenometry, and it rests on the idea that a living thing can be so patient that its growth becomes a unit of geological measurement. Some individual lichens are estimated to be thousands of years old. A patch you could cover with your palm might predate every building in the town where it grows.

Lichens are also absurdly tough. They live in Antarctic dry valleys, on desert rocks that bake by day and freeze by night, on the bare surfaces of new lava. Many can dry out almost completely, suspending their metabolism, and then revive within minutes when water returns. In 2005, researchers sent lichens into orbit and exposed them directly to space for about two weeks: vacuum, cosmic radiation, ultraviolet light unfiltered by atmosphere. When they came back, they resumed photosynthesizing. There is something almost comic about this. The crust on the churchyard wall could, in a sense, survive a trip outside the spacecraft that most of us could not.

And yet, for all their toughness, many lichens are exquisitely sensitive to one thing: air pollution. Because they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, with no roots and no protective waxy skin, they soak up whatever is floating around, including sulfur dioxide. In industrial Britain, lichens vanished from the trunks of trees near cities. This, incidentally, is part of the famous peppered moth story: the pale, lichen-camouflaged moths became conspicuous on bare, soot-darkened bark, and dark moths flourished. When clean-air laws took effect, lichens slowly returned, and ecologists now use them as living air-quality monitors. A tree trunk shaggy with lichen is a small certificate that the air nearby is reasonably clean.

So here is an organism that can survive the vacuum of space but not the exhaust of a coal plant, a being that is really several beings, that grows so slowly it measures glaciers, and that we mostly scrape off our garden furniture.

I think lichens are a good corrective to a certain way of seeing. We tend to value what is fast, large, and singular: the redwood, the eagle, the individual genius. Lichens are none of these. They are slow, small, and collective. They succeed not by dominating their environment but by forming partnerships so complete that the partners become a new kind of thing. They are pioneers, often the first life to colonize bare rock, and over centuries they help break that rock into soil in which other things can grow. Much of the living world is built, quite literally, on their patience.

Next time you pass an old wall or a weathered headstone, it might be worth stopping for a moment. What looks like a stain is a negotiation that has been going on, in some form, for hundreds of millions of years, and the one on that particular stone may have been working quietly since before anyone now alive was born.
